module.title: Unit Economics & Product Discovery
module.subtitle: 70+ EXERCISES / 6 HOURS OF PRACTICE
module.description: Can the product make money per customer? Build a unit-economics model — CAC, LTV, margin, payback — in an editable grid. Case: Calmly meditation app subscription.

lesson.title: Does Each Customer Make Us Money?
lesson.note: Uses an econ-grid widget: an editable table of labeled cells (some given, some computed by the learner) plus a scenario panel. Fixture-driven from config.cells. Learner computes values in the grid, then answers the multiple-choice. Same grading model. Numbers are round for teaching.

blocks.markdown: Hi, I'm Sam from BizOps. A product can have millions of users and still be a money pit. **Unit economics** asks a simple question: does one average customer earn more than they cost? Let's build the model for **Calmly Premium** together.
Start with **CAC** (Customer Acquisition Cost). Last month we spent **$40,000** on marketing and acquired **2,000** paying customers. What's CAC?
CAC = $40,000 / 2,000 = **$20**. Blended CAC uses total spend ÷ total new customers. (Paid-only CAC would exclude organic signups — worth separating later.)
Calmly Premium costs **$10/month**. But payment fees + content licensing eat **30%**. What's the **gross margin per subscriber per month** in dollars?
$10 × (1 − 0.30) = **$7** gross margin/month. LTV is built on *margin*, not revenue — the $3 of variable cost never reaches you. Confusing price with margin is a classic error.
How long does a subscriber stay? Our monthly churn is **5%**. Average **lifetime in months ≈ 1 / churn**. What's the average customer lifetime?
1 / 0.05 = **20 months**. This is a handy approximation: lower churn → longer lifetime → more value. A 5%→4% churn improvement moves lifetime from 20 to 25 months — a big deal, as you'll see.
Now **LTV** (Lifetime Value) = gross margin/month × lifetime. Using $7/month and 20 months, what's LTV?
$7 × 20 = **$140**. If you got $200 you used *price* ($10) instead of *margin* ($7) — a very common overstatement of LTV. Always build LTV from contribution margin.
The headline ratio investors ask about: **LTV / CAC**. With LTV $140 and CAC $20, what is it — and is that good?

options.label: 7.0 — very healthy (rule of thumb: 3+ is good)
7.0 — but we should probably spend more to grow

blocks.markdown: $140 / $20 = **7.0**. Above ~3 is generally healthy. Interestingly, a ratio *this* high can mean you're **under-investing** in acquisition — there may be room to spend more per customer and still profit. (That's the partial-credit nuance.)
Cash matters too. **CAC payback** = how many months of gross margin to earn back the $20 CAC. At $7/month margin?

$20 / $7 ≈ **2.9 months**. Payback is a *cash* view: even with great LTV/CAC, a long payback strains a startup's runway because you front the CAC now and recover it slowly. Under ~12 months is comfortable for subscriptions.
Growth proposes a new channel at **CAC $60**. Same $140 LTV. They say 'LTV still beats CAC, so ship it.' What's the sharper read?

options.label: LTV/CAC falls to ~2.3 and payback stretches to ~8.6 months — viable but much weaker; scrutinize before scaling
Ship — any channel where LTV > CAC is equally good
Reject — CAC over $50 is always bad

blocks.markdown: $140/$60 ≈ 2.3 (below the ~3 comfort line) and payback ≈ 8.6 months. 'LTV > CAC' is a low bar — the *ratio* and *payback* decide whether a channel is worth scaling. Not all profitable channels are equally good.
Leadership wants to improve unit economics. Two levers: cut CAC 10% (to $18) OR reduce churn from 5% to 4%. Which has the bigger impact on **LTV/CAC**?

options.label: Reducing churn — lifetime 20→25 months lifts LTV to $175 and LTV/CAC to ~8.75, beating the CAC cut (~7.8)
Cutting CAC — it's the direct cost

blocks.markdown: Retention compounds: 5%→4% churn stretches lifetime 20→25 months, LTV $140→$175, ratio ~8.75 vs ~7.8 for the CAC cut. This is why retention is often the highest-leverage lever in a subscription business — it multiplies every future month.
Last check — a reality caveat. Our model assumes constant 5% churn forever and that every cohort behaves the same. Why hold the LTV number loosely?

options.label: Churn isn't constant, cohorts differ, and discounting future cash matters — LTV is an estimate with assumptions, not a fact
It's exact — the formula is math

blocks.markdown: The `1/churn` LTV is a clean approximation but real churn varies by cohort and declines over time for survivors; strictly you'd also discount future margin to present value. Use the model to compare decisions, not as a precise prophecy. Good PMs know their assumptions.

That's the whole engine: CAC, gross margin, lifetime, LTV, LTV/CAC, and payback — plus the judgment to know retention compounds and LTV is an estimate. You can now sanity-check whether a product actually makes money per customer, which is what turns a feature idea into a business case.
